total:
\(\mathrm{Q}(f^{\otimes k}) = \tilde\Theta\big(k\,\mathrm{Q}(f)\big) \text{ for Boolean } f\) total Gap #

Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\mathrm{Q}(f^{\otimes k}) = O\big(k\,\mathrm{Q}(f)\log k\big)\)
    Same amplify-and-union-bound as the randomized case.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{Q}(f^{\otimes k}) = \tilde\Omega\big(k\,\mathrm{Q}(f)\big) \text{ for Boolean } f\)
    ACGT09 Reichardt11 JainKlauckSantha10
    Not proved directly: the general adversary bound has direct sum behaviour [ACGT09] (see also Theorem 7.2 of the long version of [Reichardt11]), and $\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}$ is tight for $\mathrm{Q}$ up to a log factor on Boolean functions [Reichardt11]. Combining the two gives a direct sum theorem up to that log, as observed by [JainKlauckSantha10]. Note the adversary bound needs a Boolean "connection" function such as XOR, so the argument does not reach relations.
  • \(\text{DPT: any } \Omega(\mathrm{Q}(f)k)\text{-query quantum algorithm computes } f^{\otimes k} \text{ with probability } 2^{-\Omega(k)}\)
    LeeRoland13 KSdW07 Spalek08
    [LeeRoland13], for possibly non-Boolean $f$, with a threshold version for Boolean $f$; it improves [KSdW07], whose budget scaled as $\sqrt{\mathrm{bs}(f)}k$, and the multiplicative-adversary DPT of [Spalek08], whose budget scaled with that measure instead. The quantum DPT therefore arrived at the right scale before the classical one, and the two are incomparable as statements about randomized algorithms: [Drucker12] allows a larger query budget, [LeeRoland13] a larger class of algorithms.

A tight direct sum for $\mathrm{Q}$ -- without the log, and for relations -- is open problem 2 of [JainKlauckSantha10]. This is the one place where the quantum world is less clean than the classical one: $\mathrm{D}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ both have exact or constant-factor direct sums for relations, while $\mathrm{Q}$ has neither.

see also: \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\), comp-Q, dirsum-R, dirprod-R, Direct sum and direct product, How hard is it to solve … copies? data/relations/04-composition.yaml
partial:
\(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f) \text{ as } \varepsilon\to 0\) partial Settled parameter: eps #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{Q}_\varepsilon(f) = O\big(\mathrm{Q}(f)\log(1/\varepsilon)\big)\)
    Repetition + majority, exactly as classically.
  • \(\mathrm{Q}_\varepsilon(\mathrm{OR}_N) = \Theta\big(\sqrt{N\log(1/\varepsilon)}\big)\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{OR}_n\) BCWZ99
    Quantum amplification is cheaper: $\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$ rather than $\log(1/\varepsilon)$, against the classical $\Theta(N\log(1/\varepsilon))$.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{Q}_\varepsilon(\mathrm{OR}_N) = \Omega\big(\sqrt{N\log(1/\varepsilon)}\big)\)
    BCWZ99

So the "hidden constant in $\varepsilon$" is a different function of $\varepsilon$ in the quantum and classical worlds. Any statement of the form "$\mathrm{R}=O(\mathrm{Q}^c)$" that hides $\varepsilon$-dependence is hiding a genuine phenomenon.

see also: \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{OR}_n\), \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), [BCWZ99] data/relations/07-parameters.yaml

params.name: eps
params.dependence: $\mathrm{Q}_\varepsilon(f) = O(\mathrm{Q}(f)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ by majority voting. For decision problems the $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ is sometimes removable via amplitude amplification when the algorithm has one-sided structure. In the small-bias regime $\varepsilon = 1/2-\gamma$ one has $\mathrm{Q}(f) = O(\gamma^{-1}\mathrm{Q}_{1/2-\gamma}(f))$ -- note $\gamma^{-1}$, not $\gamma^{-2}$: amplitude amplification is quadratically better than classical majority voting, which is the source of several quantum/classical gaps.

comp:
\(\mathrm{Q}(f\circ g) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{Q}(f)\,\mathrm{Q}(g)\big)\) partial Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{Q}(f\circ g) = O(\mathrm{Q}(f)\,\mathrm{Q}(g))\)
    LMRSS11 Reichardt11
    Via $\mathrm{Q}=\Theta(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm})$ and the perfect composition of the SDP; no $\log$ factor, in sharp contrast to the randomized case.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{Q}(f\circ g) = \Omega(\mathrm{Q}(f)\,\mathrm{Q}(g))\)
    HLS07 Reichardt11

Quantum query complexity is the only major measure in this zoo that composes perfectly for partial functions. This is the deep reason the quantum world is better behaved, and the reason $\mathrm{R}^{*}(f)=\Omega(\mathrm{Q}(f))$.

see also: \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}^{*}(f)\), comp-R data/relations/04-composition.yaml
facts: $\mathrm{D}(f) = O(\mathrm{Q}(f)^4)$ for total $f$ [ABKRT21], improving $O(\mathrm{Q}^6)$; matching separation $\mathrm{D}=\tilde\Omega(\mathrm{Q}^4)$ [ABBLSS17], so the exponent is 4, settled.

$\mathrm{R}(f) \le \mathrm{D}(f) = O(\mathrm{Q}(f)^4)$ for total $f$; best known separation $\mathrm{R}=\tilde\Omega(\mathrm{Q}^3)$ [BansalSinha21, SSW21], so the $\mathrm{R}$-vs-$\mathrm{Q}$ exponent lies in $[3,4]$.
For partial functions the gap with $\mathrm{R}$ is unbounded: $\mathrm{Q}=O(1)$ vs $\mathrm{R}=\tilde\Omega(n^{1-1/2k})$; exponential for Simon's problem.
self.name: Bounded-error quantum query complexity
self.short: Number of applications of the phase/bit oracle O_x needed to compute f with error <= eps.

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{Q}(f) \le \mathrm{Q}^{\mathrm{rob}}(f)\)
    BNRdW05
    A perfect oracle is a noisy oracle that happens never to err, so a robust algorithm may be run against it unchanged -- or, in the "noisy copies" formulation, the copies are prepared from the perfect oracle at no extra query cost.

The reverse is the theorem: $\mathrm{Q}^{\mathrm{rob}}(f) = O(\mathrm{Q}(f)\log \mathrm{Q}(f))$ [BNRdW05], and for $\mathrm{PARITY}$ the logarithm is not needed but the linear term is -- robustness is nearly free for quantum algorithms, unlike the classical $\mathrm{N}_p$ story.
